questions.prompt: In a cell membrane bilayer, which way do the phospholipids arrange themselves?

options.a: Heads that avoid water face inward, and tails that love water face outward.
options.b: Tails that love water face outward, and heads that avoid water face the water.
options.c: Heads that love water face the water on both sides, and tails are tucked inside.
options.d: Heads and tails both avoid water equally, so they face the inside of the membrane.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that a phospholipid is amphipathic?

options.a: It has only water-loving parts.
options.b: It has water-loving heads and water-avoiding tails.
options.c: It has only saturated tails.
options.d: It has sugars on its outer surface.

questions.prompt: Which kind of fatty acid tail packs closely in a membrane?

options.a: Saturated tails, which pack closely.
options.b: Unsaturated tails, because double bonds straighten them.
options.c: Unsaturated tails, because double bonds let them pack tightly.
options.d: Water-loving heads, which face inward.

questions.prompt: What effect do double bonds have in unsaturated fatty acid tails?

options.a: Tighter packing and lower fluidity.
options.b: Stiffer tails that resist all movement.
options.c: Tails that switch leaflets more often.
options.d: Kinks that hinder close packing and increase fluidity.

questions.prompt: Which set lists factors that affect membrane fluidity?

options.a: Temperature only.
options.b: Tail saturation, chain length, temperature, and cholesterol.
options.c: Only the sugars on the outer surface.
options.d: Only the number of leaflets.

questions.prompt: Sugars on the outer surface of a cell form the glycocalyx. What is one role the glycocalyx plays?

options.a: Helping cells recognize one another and tell self from non-self.
options.b: Pulling lipids into the inner leaflet.
options.c: Making the tails of phospholipids kink.
options.d: Forming the water-avoiding tails of the bilayer.

questions.prompt: In a very fluid membrane, what does cholesterol do?

options.a: Increases movement of membrane components.
options.c: Adds water-loving heads to the bilayer.
options.d: Makes the membrane stiffen further even when it is already very fluid.

questions.prompt: Why is cholesterol useful when the membrane is cold?

options.a: It increases fluidity in the cold.
options.b: It causes excessive stiffening in the cold.
options.c: It prevents excessive stiffening in the cold.
options.d: It moves lipids across the leaflets.

questions.prompt: Which description matches the fluid mosaic model?

options.a: Fixed proteins arranged in rigid layers.
options.b: Two identical leaflets with no moving parts.
options.c: A bilayer made only of sugars.
options.d: A mixture of lipids, cholesterol, and proteins whose components can move sideways.

questions.prompt: Lipids rarely switch between the two leaflets of a membrane unless certain molecules are present. Which ones?

options.a: Water molecules.
options.c: Enzymes such as flippases, floppases, and scramblases.
options.d: Double bonds in the tails.

payload.explanation_text: A cell membrane is a flexible boundary. Phospholipids have water-loving heads and water-avoiding tails: this combination is called amphipathic. They form a bilayer with heads toward water on both sides and tails tucked inside. Saturated fatty acid tails pack closely. Double bonds kink unsaturated tails, making close packing harder and increasing fluidity. Fluidity describes how freely membrane components move. Tail saturation, chain length, temperature, and cholesterol affect it. Cholesterol buffers fluidity: it restrains movement when the membrane is very fluid and prevents excessive stiffening in the cold. The fluid mosaic model describes a mixture of lipids, cholesterol, and proteins whose components can move sideways. The two membrane layers, or leaflets, differ in composition. Lipids rarely switch leaflets without enzymes such as flippases, floppases, and scramblases. Sugars on the outer surface form the glycocalyx and help cells recognize one another, including distinguishing self from non-self.
